concept.name: Read Repair & Anti-Entropy

relationships.description: Connects Read Repair & Anti-Entropy to caching in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Read repair and anti-entropy background repair heal divergent replicas in eventually consistent distributed stores—read repair fixes stale keys on the hot read path, while anti-entropy reconciles entire key ranges offline using Merkle trees.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use read repair for fast, opportunistic healing of hot keys during `QUORUM` reads, and schedule periodic Merkle-tree anti-entropy repairs (`nodetool repair`) faster than `gc_grace_seconds` (e.g., < 10 days) to prevent deleted tombstones from resurrecting.

concept.whyItMatters: In AP/leaderless databases like Cassandra, ScyllaDB, DynamoDB-style rings, and Riak, network partitions and node restarts inevitably leave replicas out of sync. Without both read repair and anti-entropy, cold data rots silently and expired tombstones can resurrect deleted records ('zombie data').
whenToUse: Leaderless or multi-master quorum stores (`N=3, W=2, R=2`) where any replica can accept writes while peers are temporarily unreachable.
Read-heavy workloads needing low-overhead healing of active keys via digest comparison on quorum reads.
Operational clusters requiring full-dataset convergence across cold keys, dropped hints, and tombstone cleanup.
whenNotToUse: Single-leader strongly consistent systems (PostgreSQL synchronous replication, Spanner, Raft/Paxos) where followers apply an ordered WAL/log.
Read-repair on `CL=ONE` reads if strict latency predictability is required and background repair is already frequent—though probabilistic repair is still helpful.
Running full-cluster anti-entropy repairs during peak traffic without I/O throttling, which saturates disk compaction and network bandwidth.
keyPoints: Blocking (synchronous) read repair compares a full data read from 1 replica against cryptographic digests from `R-1` replicas; on mismatch, it fetches full values, resolves by timestamp/version vector, and writes the winner back before returning.
Asynchronous read repair returns the response immediately after `CL=ONE` or `QUORUM` and repairs divergent replicas in the background.
Hinted handoff buffers missed writes for a brief outage (typically `max_hint_window = 3h`), but is a best-effort optimization—not a substitute for anti-entropy.
Anti-entropy (e.g., Cassandra `nodetool repair`) builds Merkle trees over token ranges on each replica, exchanging hashes to pinpoint divergent key buckets in O(log N) network traffic.
Tombstone resurrection occurs if a node misses a delete and isn't repaired before `gc_grace_seconds` (default 10 days / 864,000s) purges the tombstone on peers.

examples.title: Preventing Zombie Deletes in Apache Cassandra
examples.scenario: A 12-node Cassandra cluster (`RF=3`, `gc_grace_seconds=864000`) had a node down for 4 hours during a `DELETE` wave, exceeding `max_hint_window_in_ms` (3h). `nodetool repair` had been disabled for 3 weeks.
examples.outcome: Peers purged tombstones after 10 days; when the stale node was later read with `QUORUM`, read repair propagated the old un-deleted row back to all 3 replicas. Scheduling weekly incremental repairs via Cassandra Reaper eliminated zombie data.

examples.title: Digest-Optimized Quorum Read Repair
examples.scenario: A user-profile service queries Cassandra at `LOCAL_QUORUM` (`R=2` of `RF=3`) with 16 KB JSON blobs at 30,000 reads/sec.
examples.outcome: Sending 1 full data request + 1 MD5/SHA digest request cuts read-path network bandwidth by ~45% when replicas agree, while triggering full-row reconciliation only on the <0.2% of reads with a digest mismatch.

tradeOffs.pro: Blocking read repair guarantees monotonic reads—subsequent reads at `QUORUM` see the repaired value immediately.
tradeOffs.con: Adds an extra round-trip (fetching full rows + writing repairs) to tail latency whenever a mismatch occurs.

tradeOffs.pro: Incremental repair only hashes newly written SSTables, cutting repair CPU and disk I/O by 80-90%.
tradeOffs.con: Requires careful SSTable anti-compaction management and can complicate streaming during node replacements.

tradeOffs.pro: LWW (Cassandra wall-clock timestamps) resolves conflicts in O(1) without client intervention.
tradeOffs.con: NTP clock skew between coordinators can silently discard newer writes; version vectors (Riak) preserve siblings but shift merge logic to clients.

failureModes.name: Zombie Data (Tombstone Resurrection)
failureModes.description: A replica misses a delete, peers purge the tombstone after `gc_grace_seconds`, and a subsequent read repair treats the stale value as live data.
failureModes.mitigation: Run full or incremental anti-entropy repair strictly within `gc_grace_seconds` (e.g., every 3-5 days for a 10-day grace period).

failureModes.name: Merkle Tree Hash-Bucket Amplification
failureModes.description: In large partitions/ranges, a fixed-depth Merkle tree (`depth=15`, 32,768 leaves) groups thousands of keys per leaf; a single stale key forces streaming an entire leaf bucket.
failureModes.mitigation: Use sub-range repairs (`-st` / `-et` token ranges via Cassandra Reaper) and keep partition sizes under 100 MB.

failureModes.name: Coordinator Clock Skew Overwriting Newer Data
failureModes.description: Under LWW conflict resolution, a coordinator whose clock is 2 seconds ahead stamps an older logical write with a higher timestamp, causing read repair to overwrite newer data.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce strict NTP/chrony sync (`< 10 ms` drift) across all nodes and alert on clock-skew metrics, or use HLC/version vectors.

failureModes.name: Repair-Induced Disk & Compaction Storm
failureModes.description: Running unthrottled `nodetool repair` across all nodes simultaneously spikes disk reads for Merkle tree generation and floods SSTables.
failureModes.mitigation: Stagger sub-range repairs with an orchestrator (Reaper), throttle `stream_throughput_outbound`, and run during off-peak windows.

commonMistakes: Relying solely on read repair for consistency—cold keys that are rarely read will never heal.
Assuming hinted handoff guarantees consistency; hints expire after `max_hint_window` (3 hours default) or drop on node crash.
Setting `gc_grace_seconds` to `0` on tables that receive `DELETE`s or TTLs, guaranteeing zombie resurrection on any transient outage.
Running `nodetool repair` simultaneously on every node in a ring, causing duplicate work and cluster-wide I/O saturation.
Using `CL=ONE` reads with `read_repair` disabled while expecting monotonic read-your-writes consistency.

sections.content:
## The idea

In leaderless replicated databases (Dynamo-style rings like Cassandra, ScyllaDB, and Riak), there is no single primary log ordering every write. If a replica is temporarily unreachable during a `QUORUM` write, it misses the mutation. Two complementary mechanisms restore convergence:

- **Read repair (hot path)**: Opportunistically detects and heals divergent replicas *during normal client reads* using lightweight digest comparisons.
- **Anti-entropy repair (background)**: Proactively scans *all* key ranges—including cold data never touched by reads—using Merkle trees to find and stream missing mutations before tombstones expire.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a `LOCAL_QUORUM` (`R=2` of `RF=3`) read on key `user:42` where Replica A and B hold `v2 (ts=200)` and Replica C missed the write and holds `v1 (ts=100)`:

1. **Digest optimization**: The coordinator sends a **full data read** to the fastest replica (Replica A) and a **cryptographic digest request** to Replica C.
2. **Mismatch detected**: Replica A returns `{val: v2, ts: 200, digest: 0x9f}` while Replica C returns `{digest: 0x3a}` (`0x9f != 0x3a`).
3. **Full read & resolution**: The coordinator requests the full row from Replica C, compares timestamps (`ts=200 > ts=100`), and selects `v2` as the winner.
4. **Blocking repair write**: The coordinator issues a repair write of `v2 (ts=200)` to Replica C and awaits acknowledgment before returning `v2` to the client.
5. **Cold-key safety net**: For keys never read, a weekly **Merkle-tree anti-entropy** job exchanges tree hashes between A, B, and C, streaming only the mismatched token sub-ranges.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Merkle trees, hints, and tombstone lifecycle
sections.content:
## Merkle trees, hints, and tombstone lifecycle

- **Hinted handoff**: When Replica C is down for a few minutes, the coordinator stores a local *hint* (up to `max_hint_window = 3h`) and replays it once C recovers. If C stays down longer or the coordinator crashes, hints are lost.
- **Merkle tree anti-entropy**: Each replica builds a binary hash tree over a token range (e.g., Cassandra uses depth 15 = $32,768$ leaf buckets). Nodes compare root hashes; if equal, the range is in sync in $O(1)$ network traffic. If unequal, they walk down differing branches and stream only the mismatched leaf ranges.
- **Tombstone safety**: Deletes write a tombstone marker retained for `gc_grace_seconds` (default 10 days). Anti-entropy **must** complete across all replicas within this window so no node retains pre-delete values after peers purge the tombstone.

## Consistency healing mechanisms compared

| Mechanism | Trigger | Scope | Network Cost | Prevents Zombie Deletes? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hinted Handoff | Replica unreachable on write | Recent missed writes (< 3h) | Low (replay on recovery) | No (hints expire) |
| Blocking Read Repair | `QUORUM` read digest mismatch | Hot keys being read | 1x full + `(R-1)` digests | Only if key is read before `gc_grace` |
| Async Read Repair | Probabilistic on reads | Sampled hot keys | Background repair writes | No guarantee for cold keys |
| Merkle Anti-Entropy | Scheduled (`nodetool repair`) | Full token ranges (hot + cold) | $O(\log N)$ hashes + diff stream | **Yes**, if run `< gc_grace_seconds` |

## Failure modes

- **Zombie data resurrection**: Missing an anti-entropy cycle beyond `gc_grace_seconds` allows stale replicas to re-inject deleted rows via read repair.
- **Clock-skew LWW data loss**: Coordinator NTP drift causes older writes to carry higher timestamps, making read repair overwrite newer mutations.
- **Repair I/O starvation**: Unthrottled Merkle tree validation scans all SSTables, triggering compaction backlogs and p99 read spikes.
- **Wide-partition Merkle bloat**: A single 1 GB partition forces the entire leaf bucket to stream even when only 1 KB differs.

## Production patterns & observability

- **Automated sub-range orchestration**: Use tools like **Cassandra Reaper** or ScyllaDB Manager to split repairs into small token segments, pausing automatically when cluster latency or pending compactions spike.
- **Incremental repairs**: Enable incremental repair (`-inc` in modern Cassandra 4.x+) so already-repaired SSTables are skipped on subsequent runs.
- **Alert on repair age**: Track `time_since_last_repair_seconds` per keyspace and page if it exceeds `0.5 * gc_grace_seconds`.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Use `LOCAL_QUORUM` (`R + W > RF`) with blocking read repair for strong monotonic reads on active keys.
- [ ] Schedule automated sub-range anti-entropy repairs at least every 3-5 days when `gc_grace_seconds` is 10 days.
- [ ] Never set `gc_grace_seconds = 0` on tables with `DELETE`s or TTL expirations.
- [ ] Throttle repair streaming bandwidth and monitor compaction pending tasks during repair windows.
- [ ] Enforce NTP/chrony sync (`< 10 ms` drift) across all coordinator and storage nodes if using LWW.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Read Repair Anti Entropy

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Read repair and anti-entropy background repair heal divergent replicas in eventually consistent distributed stores—read repair fixes stale keys on the hot read path, while anti-entropy reconciles entire key ranges offline using Merkle trees.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Replica A (Fast) applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Replica C (Stale).

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Replica C (Stale) experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Run full or incremental anti-entropy repair strictly within `gc_grace_seconds` (e.g., every 3-5 days for a 10-day grace period).

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Use read repair for fast, opportunistic healing of hot keys during `QUORUM` reads, and schedule periodic Merkle-tree anti-entropy repairs (`nodetool repair`) faster than `gc_grace_seconds` (e.g., < 10 days) to prevent deleted tombstones from resurrecting.
Avoid trap: Relying solely on read repair for consistency—cold keys that are rarely read will never heal.
Avoid trap: Assuming hinted handoff guarantees consistency; hints expire after `max_hint_window` (3 hours default) or drop on node crash.
When to reach for it: Leaderless or multi-master quorum stores (`N=3, W=2, R=2`) where any replica can accept writes while peers are temporarily unreachable.
When to reach for it: Read-heavy workloads needing low-overhead healing of active keys via digest comparison on quorum reads.

putItTogether.title: Putting Read Repair Anti Entropy Together
putItTogether.summary: Use read repair for fast, opportunistic healing of hot keys during `QUORUM` reads, and schedule periodic Merkle-tree anti-entropy repairs (`nodetool repair`) faster than `gc_grace_seconds` (e.g., < 10 days) to prevent deleted tombstones from resurrecting.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Read Repair Anti Entropy before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Peers purged tombstones after 10 days; when the stale node was later read with `QUORUM`, read repair propagated the old un-deleted row back to all 3 replicas. Scheduling weekly incremental repairs via Cassandra Reaper eliminated zombie data.
